author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell reacts to Ursula von der Leyen and the growing power of European bureaucracy, arguing that control is increasingly presented as care. From savings and digital IDs to pandemic-era restrictions, he jokes about how modern authority rarely announces itself as authoritarian — it simply tells you it’s here to help. Beneath the humor is a bigger warning about what happens when convenience, security and bureaucracy begin to erode individual freedom.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Anne Hathaway describes abortion as something that can represent “mercy,” prompting Russell to reflect on his own past and question the way abortion is framed as a political battle. Drawing on the experience of being offered a late-term abortion after his son's congenital heart condition was discovered, he asks what happens when personal convenience collides with the principle that life is sacred.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell draws an unexpected line connecting Princess Diana, 9/11, Covid, and even a blockbuster movie, arguing they all got shaped by the exact same media playbook. His sharpest point lands on how convenient facts quietly replace the real ones, whether it's a Titanic movie detail nobody questions or a decades old pattern in how the press builds a story around a person rather than reports on them.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell breaks down the strict discipline behind his daily life, staying constantly conscious of what he eats, says, and does, and deliberately exposing himself to extremes every day, cold therapy, heat, and Brazilian jiu jitsu included. He credits Michael Singer for a mindset shift that carries him through it all, that the moment in front of you isn't what's bothering you, you're bothering yourself about it. He also opens up about why jiu jitsu specifically means so much to him, tracing it back to an ancient, anthropological kind of trust between people, the same trust built through touch and struggle long before modern life pulled us apart from each other. A genuinely thoughtful look at the discipline behind Russell's day to day.

author: Russell Brand
description:
A Stanford developed test found that 96 percent of people who tested PCR positive without symptoms weren't actually infectious, meaning nearly all of them posed no real risk to anyone else. That test was available as early as May 2020, right at the start of the pandemic, yet the CDC and other health authorities did nothing with it, never adopting it or using it to ease unnecessary restrictions on asymptomatic people. Russell's panel makes the obvious point, an agency that spent the entire pandemic insisting everyone follow the science apparently wasn't all that interested in a real scientific test that could have changed everything.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Fifty years ago, Johnson & Johnson itself flagged that a small amount of asbestos was present in its baby powder, and the FDA spent decades studying how much should even be allowed, all while continuing to permit it. It took more than five decades, and a significant number of cancer diagnoses along the way, before the company finally acknowledged what it had known internally the entire time and removed asbestos from the product. A sobering look at how long a known risk can sit in plain sight before anything actually changes.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell describes surrender to Christ in strikingly modern terms, the creator of the simulation entering the simulation itself, and lands on a line that reframes his entire public identity, that he's no longer in the business of being Russell Brand, he's in the business of serving Jesus Christ. He's honest that the idea keeps him alive, but just as honest that old egotism still creeps back in whenever it gets the chance. A raw, philosophically sharp moment on what real surrender actually costs.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell closes with a genuinely striking prayer, acknowledging the contradictions of occupying a monetized, compromised space, before asking for protection over political leaders he disagrees with and even nations he'd call enemies. He prays for salvation for those we'd go to war with, comfort for anyone broken by bullets and bombs, and peace over people who wish him harm personally. A quietly powerful moment of humility and grace in a world he describes as increasingly defined by conflict and hatred.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell tells the story of interviewing Mike Tyson about losing 300 million dollars and deciding, for reasons even he can't fully explain, to push the joke a little too far. He watches Tyson's expression change in real time as he pushes deeper into the joke about buying white tigers, right up until Tyson calmly tells him he could throw him out the window, and Russell's response says it all. A hilarious, slightly terrifying story about knowing exactly when to stop and choosing not to.
